headline: Chinook salmon reclaim 200 miles of river in stunning comeback
meta_description: After four dams were removed from Oregon's Klamath River in 2024, over 13,000 Chinook salmon returned to spawn, reclaiming habitat lost for a century.
summary_short: Chinook salmon are making a dramatic return to the Klamath River following dam removal, reclaiming 200 miles of spawning habitat that had been blocked for generations.
body:
When four dams were removed from the Klamath River in 2024, something remarkable happened: more than 13,000 Chinook salmon rushed upstream in 2025, navigating rapids and engineered fishways to reach habitats sealed off from them for over a century. The fish expanded into 345 kilometers of formerly blocked river, recolonizing 88% of their known historical habitat in the Southern Oregon and Northern California waterway. This speed of recovery stunned the scientists who study them, including researcher Damon Goodman, who noted that the fish "felt like we were running to keep up with the fish."

To document this unexpected surge, Goodman's team deployed specialized underwater sonar cameras—essentially video equipment that sees through murky water using sound waves rather than light. Installing the camera near the former Iron Gate Dam site, they could distinguish individual Chinook from other fish species and measure their size, all while the river remained too turbid for traditional monitoring. The technology proved essential for capturing what would otherwise have remained invisible: the quiet, powerful return of thousands of salmon finding their way home.

Yet the celebration is tempered by realism. The Klamath River's salmon population had declined roughly 90% over the 20th century due to damming, and reaching historical population levels will require successful reproduction across multiple generations alongside improvements in water quality and habitat conditions throughout the basin. As Goodman cautioned, dam removal was "an enormous step forward, but it doesn't eliminate all the challenges facing salmon." Still, the fish themselves have delivered an unmistakable message: given the chance, they will return.
quick_facts: 13,000+ Chinook salmon migrated upstream in 2025 after dam removal
Fish recolonized 345 km (214 miles) of formerly blocked habitat
Sonar cameras documented fish movement through turbid river water
Four Klamath River dams removed in 2024, opening century-old barrier
